title: Topic Drill: Sentence Structure, Grammar and Punctuation (Set C)

items.stem:
The Harlow Ridge wind farm began feeding power to the county grid in March. Crews now inspect each turbine every quarter. Because the blades spin faster in winter storms and the gearboxes face heavier loads.

Which choice best describes the last sentence of this maintenance notice?
options: It is a run-on, because two complete sentences are joined with no punctuation at all.
It is a fragment, because the subordinate clause has no main clause attached to it.
It is a comma splice, because a comma joins two independent clauses in the notice.
It is a complete sentence, because it contains both a subject and a verb in each part.
items.explanation: The sentence opens with because, which makes the whole group of words a dependent clause that cannot stand alone. It needs a main clause, such as the inspections are more frequent. It is not a run-on or comma splice, since no two independent clauses meet. Having a subject and verb does not make it complete.

items.stem:
The control room at the Harlow Ridge wind farm tracks output every hour. A senior operator reviews the logs each morning before the shift change.

Which revision corrects the error in this sentence from the log summary: The turbines reported steady output overnight, the operators noted no drop below the forecast?
options: The turbines reported steady output overnight; the operators noted no drop below the forecast.
The turbines reported steady output overnight, therefore the operators noted no drop below the forecast.
The turbines reported steady output overnight the operators noted no drop below the forecast.
The turbines reported steady output overnight, however the operators noted no drop below the forecast.
items.explanation: The original joins two independent clauses with only a comma, which is a comma splice. A semicolon properly links two closely related complete clauses. Removing the comma creates a run-on. Adding therefore or however after a comma still leaves a comma splice, since those words are conjunctive adverbs and need a semicolon before them.

items.stem:
An engineer’s report on the Harlow Ridge wind farm compares output across the site. Only the tallest towers stand along the northern ridge, where the wind is strongest.

Which sentence from the report uses the correct relative pronoun and punctuation to say that only the ridge turbines produce more power than the rest?
options: The turbines, which sit on the northern ridge, produce more power than the others.
The turbines who sit on the northern ridge produce more power than the others.
The turbines that sit on the northern ridge produce more power than the others.
The turbines, that sit on the northern ridge, produce more power than the others.
items.explanation: The clause identifies which turbines are meant, so it is restrictive and takes that with no commas. Commas with which would suggest every turbine sits on the ridge. Who refers to people, not machines. Setting off a clause that begins with that with commas is never correct, because that is used only for restrictive clauses.

items.stem:
Before every climb at the Harlow Ridge wind farm, technicians pack their gear in a canvas bag. The crew leader reads the packing list aloud to be sure nothing is missing.

Which version of the following sentence from the safety manual uses commas correctly: Technicians carried a torque wrench a harness a radio and a spare bolt kit up the tower?
options: Technicians carried a torque wrench, a harness a radio, and a spare bolt kit up the tower.
Technicians carried, a torque wrench, a harness, a radio, and a spare bolt kit, up the tower.
Technicians carried a torque wrench a harness, a radio, and, a spare bolt kit up the tower.
Technicians carried a torque wrench, a harness, a radio, and a spare bolt kit up the tower.
items.explanation: Four items in a series need a comma after each item except the last, including one before and in the standard style. The first wrong version leaves out a comma between the harness and the radio. The second puts commas around the whole series and after the verb. The third misplaces commas and puts one after and.

items.stem:
The maintenance office at the Harlow Ridge wind farm posts a checklist at the base of every tower. The list is short, and each line names a specific item for the crew to check before leaving.

Which choice shows the correct punctuation for this sentence from the checklist: The inspection checklist covers three areas, blade condition, brake wear, and cable tension?
options: The inspection checklist covers three areas: blade condition, brake wear, and cable tension.
The inspection checklist covers three areas; blade condition, brake wear, and cable tension.
The inspection checklist covers: three areas, blade condition, brake wear, and cable tension.
The inspection checklist covers three areas, blade condition; brake wear; and cable tension.
items.explanation: A colon correctly follows a complete statement and introduces the list that explains it. A semicolon cannot introduce a list of simple items, since what follows is not a complete clause. Placing the colon right after covers breaks the verb from its object. Mixing a comma and semicolons in the list is inconsistent.

items.stem:
The county weather service finished its radar upgrade in October. At the closing ceremony, the director praised everyone on the project team. One thank-you line in her speech read: The team thanked the engineer who they trusted to calibrate the dish.

Which revision corrects the pronoun in that line?
options: The team thanked the engineer whose they trusted to calibrate the dish.
The team thanked the engineer who they trusted to calibrate the dish, himself.
The team thanked the engineer whom they trusted to calibrate the dish.
The team thanked the engineer which they trusted to calibrate the dish.
items.explanation: The pronoun is the object of they trusted, so formal writing calls for whom. Whose shows possession and has no noun to modify here. Adding himself leaves the original who unchanged and adds an extra pronoun. Which refers to things, and an engineer is a person, so it is the wrong relative pronoun.

items.stem:
A weather radar upgrade means new schedules for the technicians. The site supervisor sent a short note to the staff. It said: The director gave the new maintenance schedule to Priya and I on Monday.

Which choice corrects the error in the supervisor’s sentence?
options: The director gave the new maintenance schedule to Priya and myself on Monday.
The director gave the new maintenance schedule to Priya and me on Monday.
The director gave the new maintenance schedule to Priya and she on Monday.
The director gave the new maintenance schedule to she and I on Monday.
items.explanation: Priya and the speaker are objects of the preposition to, so the object form me is needed. Dropping Priya shows the test: gave the schedule to me. Myself is a reflexive form with no matching subject. She and I are both subject forms, so they cannot follow to.

items.stem:
The weather radar upgrade at the Cedar Point station moved into testing this week. The testing crew has worked long hours to finish before the storm season. A status memo contains this sentence: The radar crew has finished its tests but they still wait for approval.

Which revision fixes the agreement problem?
options: The radar crew have finished its tests but they still wait for approval.
The radar crew has finished their tests but still waits for approval.
The radar crew has finished its tests but still wait for approval.
The radar crew has finished its tests but still waits for approval.
items.explanation: A collective noun acting as one unit takes a singular verb and the pronoun its. The key keeps both the verb and the second verb singular. The first choice mixes plural verbs with singular its. The second mixes singular has with plural their. The third leaves the second verb plural after a singular subject.

items.stem:
Each antenna in the weather radar upgrade is mounted on a heavy steel base. Engineers wrote a spec sheet that describes the parts in detail. A line on that sheet reads: Each of the new antennas have a backup motor.

Which revision corrects the error in that line?
options: Each of the new antennas are having a backup motor.
Each of the new antennas has a backup motor.
Each of the new antennas have backup motor.
Each of the new antenna have a backup motor.
items.explanation: Each is a singular indefinite pronoun, so the verb must be has, even though antennas is plural and sits near the verb. The first wrong choice swaps in a plural verb in a progressive form. The second keeps the plural verb and drops the article. The third changes antennas but keeps the plural verb.

items.stem:
A reporter visited the weather radar site at the end of the upgrade. She wrote about how fast the crew climbed the hilltop road before dawn. One sentence in her draft says: By noon the crew had drove to the hilltop site twice.

Which revision uses the correct verb form?
options: By noon the crew had driven to the hilltop site twice.
By noon the crew had drived to the hilltop site twice.
By noon the crew has drove to the hilltop site twice.
By noon the crew was driven to the hilltop site twice.
items.explanation: The past perfect tense needs had plus the past participle, and the past participle of drive is driven. Drove is the simple past form and cannot follow had. Drived is not a word, since drive is irregular. Has drove mixes tenses and the wrong form. Was driven changes the meaning to passive.

items.stem:
Volunteers spent the weekend clearing the Dunmore wetland. A neighbor wrote a short account for the community paper. One sentence reads: After the volunteers pulled the invasive reeds the water began to clear.

Where does a comma belong in the sentence?
options: After the volunteers, pulled the invasive reeds the water began to clear.
After the volunteers pulled, the invasive reeds the water began to clear.
After the volunteers pulled the invasive reeds the water, began to clear.
After the volunteers pulled the invasive reeds, the water began to clear.
items.explanation: An introductory clause that begins with after is followed by a comma before the main clause starts. The main clause here is the water began to clear. The other choices put the comma inside the introductory clause or inside the main clause, separating a subject from its verb or a verb from its object.

items.stem:
The Dunmore wetland restoration depends on careful planning of the new water channel. At a public meeting, the project manager introduced the expert who designed it. The newsletter printed: Dr. Imani Okoro the lead hydrologist explained the new channel design.

Which revision punctuates the appositive correctly?
options: Dr. Imani Okoro, the lead hydrologist explained the new channel design.
Dr. Imani Okoro the lead hydrologist, explained the new channel design.
Dr. Imani Okoro, the lead hydrologist, explained the new channel design.
Dr. Imani Okoro, the lead hydrologist, explained, the new channel design.
items.explanation: The phrase the lead hydrologist renames the speaker and adds extra information, so it needs commas on both sides. One comma alone leaves the appositive half open, either at the start or at the end. The third version adds an extra comma that separates the verb from its direct object.

items.stem:
The Dunmore wetland will reopen after months of restoration work. The parks department sent out an announcement for residents. It states: The wetland opens to the public on Saturday June 6 2026 and tours begin at nine.

Which choice uses commas correctly for the date?
options: The wetland opens to the public on Saturday June 6, 2026 and tours begin at nine.
The wetland opens to the public on Saturday, June 6, 2026, and tours begin at nine.
The wetland opens to the public on Saturday, June 6 2026, and tours begin at nine.
The wetland opens to the public on Saturday, June, 6, 2026 and tours begin at nine.
items.explanation: A full date takes a comma after the weekday and between the day and year, and a comma after the year when the sentence continues. The key also uses a comma before and, which joins two clauses. The other choices omit a required comma or insert one between the month and the day.

items.stem:
The Dunmore wetland restoration project depends on donated supplies. A volunteer coordinator wrote a thank-you note about the weekend work. It says: The restoration project’s budget covers its native plants, but the volunteers boots were bought by donation.

What is the error in this sentence?
options: The phrase volunteers boots needs an apostrophe to show possession, as in volunteers’ boots.
The word project’s should have no apostrophe, because project is already plural.
The word its should be written it’s, because the word shows possession here.
The word plants should be written plant’s, because the plants belong to the project.
items.explanation: Boots belong to the volunteers, and since volunteers is plural and ends in s, the possessive adds only an apostrophe after the s. Project’s is correctly singular possessive. Its is already the possessive form, and it’s means it is. Plants is a plain plural with no ownership.

items.stem:
A wetland restoration crew counted the animals living in the new marsh near Dunmore. A student helper wrote up the first report for the class. One line says: The restored marsh holds less frogs than the old drainage ditch did last spring.

Which revision corrects the error in word choice?
options: The restored marsh holds lesser frogs than the old drainage ditch did last spring.
The restored marsh holds fewer frogs then the old drainage ditch did last spring.
The restored marsh holds less of frogs than the old drainage ditch did last spring.
The restored marsh holds fewer frogs than the old drainage ditch did last spring.
items.explanation: Frogs can be counted one by one, so the correct comparison word is fewer. Less is used for amounts that cannot be counted, such as water. Lesser is an adjective meaning of lower importance. Then tells about time, while the comparison needs than. Less of frogs is not idiomatic.

items.stem:
The city launched a public transit app this spring. A rider posted a review explaining what she likes about it. Her review includes this sentence: The transit app shows live bus locations riders can see delays before leaving home.

Which revision best corrects the sentence boundary error?
options: The transit app shows live bus locations, riders can see delays before leaving home.
The transit app shows live bus locations, so riders can see delays before leaving home.
The transit app shows live bus locations riders, can see delays before leaving home.
The transit app shows live bus locations; so, riders can see delays before leaving home.
items.explanation: The original is a run-on, since two complete clauses meet with no punctuation or joining word. A comma plus the conjunction so fixes it and shows the cause. A comma alone creates a comma splice. Moving the comma after riders breaks the subject from its verb. A semicolon followed by so is an awkward mix.

items.stem:
The public transit app also sends alerts to riders’ phones. The development team described the feature in a short blog post. Two of its sentences were: The app sends alerts. The alerts warn riders of route changes.

Which choice combines these two sentences most effectively?
options: The app sends alerts, they warn riders of route changes.
The app sends alerts, and the alerts warn riders of route changes.
The app sends alerts that warn riders of route changes.
The app sends alerts that, they warn riders of route changes.
items.explanation: A relative clause with that folds the second sentence into the first and removes the repeated word alerts. The first wrong choice is a comma splice. The second is grammatical but repeats alerts, which is wordy. The third mixes the relative pronoun that with a leftover pronoun they and a stray comma.

items.stem:
A reviewer compared the new public transit app with the old way of checking buses. The old method gave riders only a printed sheet of times. In her review, she wrote: The old schedule listed only printed times. ____, the app updates every thirty seconds.

Which transition best fills the blank?
options: Similarly
For example
As a result
By contrast
items.explanation: The second sentence shows a difference between the paper schedule and the app, so a contrast phrase fits. Similarly would signal a likeness, which is the opposite of the meaning. For example would suggest that the app is one case of the printed schedule. As a result implies the schedule caused the update speed, which makes no sense.

items.stem:
The city’s public transit app was rebuilt over the winter. A tester wrote a short note about speed on older phones. One sentence says: The app now runs smooth on older phones.

Which revision uses the correct form of the modifier?
options: The app now runs smoothly on older phones.
The app now runs smoothest on older phones.
The app now runs more smooth on older phones.
The app now is running smooth on older phones.
items.explanation: The word describes how the app runs, so it modifies a verb and needs the adverb smoothly. Smoothest is a superlative with nothing to compare. More smooth keeps the adjective form after a verb of action. Is running smooth repeats the same adjective error in a longer verb phrase.

items.stem:
The public transit app lists stops and closures. A developer wrote an explanation for the help page. The draft sentence reads: The app lists nearby stops however it hides stops that are closed.

Which revision correctly punctuates the sentence?
options: The app lists nearby stops, however, it hides stops that are closed.
The app lists nearby stops however; it hides stops that are closed.
The app lists nearby stops; however, it hides stops that are closed.
The app lists nearby stops; however it hides stops that are closed.
items.explanation: However joins two independent clauses, so it needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it. A comma before however creates a comma splice. Putting the semicolon after however leaves the first clause hanging. The last version has the semicolon but omits the comma that sets off the transition.

items.stem:
The Eastside community kitchen needs weekend help. The manager wrote a private note to a longtime cook named Tomas. In it she said: Between you and I, the kitchen could not run without Tomas and the other volunteers.

Which revision corrects the pronoun error?
options: Between you and me, the kitchen could not run without Tomas and the other volunteers.
Between you and myself, the kitchen could not run without Tomas and the other volunteers.
Between you and him, the kitchen could not run without Tomas and the other volunteers.
Between yourself and I, the kitchen could not run without Tomas and the other volunteers.
items.explanation: The word between is a preposition, so both pronouns after it must be object forms, you and me. Myself is a reflexive form with no matching subject. Him shifts the meaning to a third person who was never named. Yourself and I mixes a reflexive with a subject form, so it is wrong.

items.stem:
Volunteers at the community kitchen share leftover rice after each dinner service. The head cook wrote a note for the supply board. It said: The cooks divided the leftover rice between the four neighborhood shelters.

Which revision uses the correct preposition?
options: The cooks divided the leftover rice amongst the four neighborhood shelter.
The cooks divided the leftover rice between each of the four neighborhood shelters.
The cooks divided the leftover rice between the neighborhood shelters of four.
The cooks divided the leftover rice among the four neighborhood shelters.
items.explanation: Among is used for three or more items, and four shelters is more than two. Between is reserved for two. The first wrong choice also drops the plural s on shelters. The second keeps between and adds each, which still fails. The third rearranges the words but keeps between.

items.stem:
The community kitchen is opening a second dining room. A newspaper intern wrote a notice about the hours. It read: The community kitchen opens it’s doors at five and closes them when the soup runs out.

Which revision corrects the error in the first clause?
options: The community kitchen opens its’ doors at five and closes them when the soup runs out.
The community kitchen opens its doors at five and closes them when the soup runs out.
The community kitchen opens it is doors at five and closes them when the soup runs out.
The community kitchen opens their doors at five and closes them when the soup runs out.
items.explanation: Its with no apostrophe is the possessive form of it, which is needed before doors. The contraction it’s means it is or it has. Its’ is not a word. Expanding it’s to it is would make the sentence nonsense. Their does not agree with the singular noun kitchen.

items.stem:
The community kitchen keeps careful records of its work. A volunteer wrote an end-of-year report for donors. One sentence in the draft reads: The kitchen has serve over four hundred meals since January.

Which revision uses the correct verb form?
options: The kitchen has been serve over four hundred meals since January.
The kitchen had serve over four hundred meals since January.
The kitchen has served over four hundred meals since January.
The kitchen has serving over four hundred meals since January.
items.explanation: The present perfect tense needs has plus the past participle, which for serve is served. The first wrong choice adds been to a base form. The second pairs had with the base form, so the participle is still missing. The third uses an incomplete progressive form with no helping verb being.

items.stem:
The Eastside community kitchen posted a volunteer request on its bulletin board. The first draft was too long, so the editor marked one sentence. It reads: At this point in time, the kitchen is currently in need of additional volunteers who can help.

Which revision is most concise without changing the meaning?
options: The kitchen is currently in need of more volunteers who can help us.
At present, the kitchen needs additional volunteers who can lend a hand.
The kitchen is now in need of more volunteers to come and help.
The kitchen needs more volunteers.
items.explanation: The original repeats the idea of time three times and says that volunteers can help, which is already implied by need. Needs more volunteers keeps the meaning in four words. The other choices keep at least one wordy phrase, such as currently in need of or lend a hand, so they still waste words.

items.stem:
The Pinewood night-sky observatory offers free programs on weekends. A flyer introduces the staff who lead them. One line on the flyer says: The observatory hired a guide that teaches children about the planets.

Which revision uses the correct relative pronoun?
options: The observatory hired a guide whom teaches children about the planets.
The observatory hired a guide, that teaches children about the planets.
The observatory hired a guide who teaches children about the planets.
The observatory hired a guide which teaches children about the planets.
items.explanation: A guide is a person, so the relative pronoun should be who, and it acts as the subject of teaches. Whom is an object form and cannot be the subject. A comma before that sets off a restrictive clause wrongly. Which refers to things or animals, not to people.

items.stem:
The night-sky observatory held a public viewing on Friday. A volunteer wrote a short entry in the visitors’ log that evening. It begins: The sky was clear on Friday, the volunteers set up four telescopes on the lawn.

Which choice best describes this sentence?
options: It is a fragment, because it lacks a verb in the second part of the sentence.
It is a comma splice, because two independent clauses are joined by only a comma.
It is correct, because the comma separates two ideas that belong together.
It has an unnecessary comma between a verb and its direct object in the first clause.
items.explanation: Each part could stand alone as a sentence, and a comma by itself cannot join them, so this is a comma splice. A period, a semicolon, or a comma plus and would fix it. Both clauses have verbs, so it is not a fragment. The comma comes after a full clause, not between a verb and its object.

items.stem:
The Pinewood observatory is old, but visitors still love it. A guide wrote a short caption for the telescope display. It uses two sentences: The telescope is old. It still produces sharp images.

Which choice combines them with the clearest logical relationship?
options: Although the telescope is old, it still produces sharp images.
The telescope is old, it still produces sharp images.
The telescope is old, because it still produces sharp images.
The telescope is old and so it still produces sharp images.
items.explanation: The two ideas contrast, so a subordinating word like although shows the relationship correctly. A bare comma leaves a splice. Because suggests that sharp images cause age, which reverses the logic. And so implies that age leads to sharp images, which is also false, so neither shows the contrast the sentences need.

items.stem:
A meteor shower brought crowds to the Pinewood observatory. The staff wrote an incident report for the board. It contains these sentences: The dome jammed, the power failed, and a guest dropped a camera. This frustrated the staff.

Which revision removes the vague pronoun in the last sentence?
options: It frustrated the staff.
This all frustrated the staff.
These setbacks frustrated the staff.
That frustrated the staff a great deal.
items.explanation: The word this could point to any one of three events, so the reader has no clear referent. A noun like setbacks names all three problems at once. It has the same vagueness with no noun at all. This all and that still lack a clear noun to point to.

items.stem:
Two guides were assigned to the late tour at the Pinewood observatory. A visitor sent a note to the front desk afterward. Part of it reads: Neither of the two guides were ready when the first visitors arrived.

Which revision corrects the agreement error?
options: Neither of the two guides were ready when the first visitor arrived.
Neither of the two guides was ready when the first visitors arrived.
Neither of the two guides are ready when the first visitors arrived.
Neither of the two guides have been ready when the first visitors arrived.
items.explanation: Neither is a singular indefinite pronoun, so it takes the singular verb was, even though guides sits close to the verb. The first wrong choice keeps were and changes a noun. The second shifts to present tense. The third uses a plural helping verb, which still disagrees with neither.

items.stem:
A river cleanup in Tamsin Falls drew a large turnout this year. A reporter wrote the opening of her article. It reads: The river cleanup drew two hundred volunteers. Including students from three schools.

Which revision best corrects the fragment?
options: The river cleanup drew two hundred volunteers, including students from three schools.
The river cleanup drew two hundred volunteers; including students from three schools.
The river cleanup drew two hundred volunteers including, students from three schools.
The river cleanup drew two hundred volunteers. Including, students from three schools.
items.explanation: The second group of words has no subject or main verb, so it is a fragment that must be attached to the first sentence. A comma before including joins it smoothly. A semicolon needs a complete clause on each side. The other choices add a comma after including or keep the period and the fragment.

items.stem:
The Tamsin Falls river cleanup gives prizes for the most trash collected. A flyer lists the rules for the contest. One line says: Whom collected the most trash bags will receive a ribbon.

Which revision corrects the pronoun error?
options: Whomever collected the most trash bags will receive a ribbon.
Whom ever collected the most trash bags will receive a ribbon.
Anyone whom collected the most trash bags will receive a ribbon.
Whoever collected the most trash bags will receive a ribbon.
items.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of collected, so it needs a subject form, who or whoever. Whomever and whom are object forms. Splitting whom ever does not fix the case. Anyone whom collected keeps the object form. Whoever is used because the whole clause acts as the subject of will receive.

items.stem:
The Tamsin Falls river cleanup needs signed forms from every school group. The organizers posted a notice for teachers. It reads: Send registration forms to the River Trust, 88 Mill Road Pell City Alabama 35125 before the deadline.

Which choice punctuates the address correctly?
options: Send registration forms to the River Trust, 88 Mill Road, Pell City, Alabama 35125, before the deadline.
Send registration forms to the River Trust, 88 Mill Road, Pell City Alabama, 35125 before the deadline.
Send registration forms to the River Trust, 88 Mill Road, Pell City, Alabama, 35125, before the deadline.
Send registration forms to the River Trust, 88 Mill Road Pell City, Alabama, 35125 before the deadline.
items.explanation: Items in an address are separated by commas, but no comma goes between the state and the zip code. A comma follows the zip code when the sentence continues. The other choices omit the comma after Mill Road, place one between the state and zip, or leave out the comma after the zip.

items.stem:
Heavy rain at Tamsin Falls pushed the river up quickly. The cleanup crew wrote a safety update for the volunteers. It said: The current has rose two feet since the rain began.

Which revision uses the correct verb form?
options: The current has raised two feet since the rain began.
The current has risen two feet since the rain began.
The current has rised two feet since the rain began.
The current had rose two feet since the rain began.
items.explanation: The present perfect uses has plus the past participle, and the past participle of rise is risen. Raised is a different verb that needs an object. Rised is not a real form. Had rose combines the wrong helping verb with a simple past form, so it fails twice in one phrase.

items.stem:
Teams came from several towns to join the Tamsin Falls river cleanup. The event newsletter listed them in a short sentence. The draft says: The cleanup attracted teams from Dover, Delaware, Salem, Oregon, and Troy, Ohio.

Which revision punctuates the list correctly?
options: The cleanup attracted teams from Dover, Delaware; Salem, Oregon, and Troy, Ohio.
The cleanup attracted teams from Dover; Delaware, Salem; Oregon, and Troy; Ohio.
The cleanup attracted teams from Dover, Delaware; Salem, Oregon; and Troy, Ohio.
The cleanup attracted teams from Dover, Delaware, Salem, Oregon; and Troy, Ohio.
items.explanation: When items in a series already contain commas, semicolons separate the items so the reader can tell where each begins and ends. The key puts a semicolon after each city and state pair. The other choices use semicolons in some places and commas in others, or split the city from its state.

items.stem:
Our school’s robotics team competed in the regional tournament last month. A team member wrote a recap for the yearbook. Two of her sentences read: The team rebuilt the arm. The judges had warned them about the weak joint.

Which choice combines these sentences most logically?
options: The team rebuilt the arm, the judges had warned them about the weak joint.
The team rebuilt the arm although the judges had warned them about the weak joint.
The team rebuilt the arm, so the judges had warned them about the weak joint.
The team rebuilt the arm because the judges had warned them about the weak joint.
items.explanation: The warning came first and caused the rebuild, so because shows the correct cause and effect. A comma alone creates a splice. Although implies a contrast that does not exist. So reverses the logic by making the warning the result of the rebuild, which is the reverse of what happened.

items.stem:
The robotics competition scored every robot on several skills. A parent wrote a short note describing how the scoring worked. One sentence says: The three judge’s scored each robot on speed and accuracy.

What is the error in the sentence?
options: The word robot should be robot’s, because the robot owns its score.
The word accuracy should be preceded by a colon, because it ends the list.
The word judge’s should be the plain plural judges, because no ownership is shown.
The word each should be replaced by every, because the judges are plural.
items.explanation: The apostrophe in judge’s wrongly makes the plural noun possessive, though nothing belongs to the judges here. Three judges simply scored the robots. Robot has no ownership, and the colon would break the phrase on speed and accuracy. Each and every are interchangeable here, so neither one is an error.

items.stem:
Two finalists reached the last round of the robotics competition. A commentator described them in the program. The draft sentence reads: Of the two finalists, the blue robot was the fastest on the final course.

Which revision uses the correct form of the comparison?
options: Of the two finalists, the blue robot was the faster on the final course.
Of the two finalists, the blue robot was the most fast on the final course.
Of the two finalists, the blue robot was the fastly on the final course.
Of the two finalists, the blue robot was the more faster on the final course.
items.explanation: Comparing two things calls for the comparative form faster, not the superlative fastest, which is for three or more. Most fast is an awkward superlative. Fastly is not a word. More faster doubles the comparison, since the ending -er already makes it comparative on its own.

items.stem:
The robotics competition judges reviewed a difficult first round. A team coach wrote this passage in the newsletter: The robot scored poorly in round one. ____, it climbed to second place after round three.

Which transition best fills the blank?
options: In addition
For instance
Because of this
Even so
items.explanation: The first sentence shows a weak start and the second shows a strong finish, so a word of contrast is needed. Even so signals that something happened in spite of the earlier result. In addition adds a similar idea. For instance introduces an example. Because of this wrongly implies the poor score caused the rise.

items.stem:
A robotics competition is a race against the clock. At the awards ceremony, a team captain told a reporter how the last repair went. His quote began: By the time the buzzer sounded, the team already finish the repairs.

Which revision uses the correct verb tense?
options: By the time the buzzer sounded, the team has already finished the repairs.
By the time the buzzer sounded, the team had already finished the repairs.
By the time the buzzer sounded, the team already finishes the repairs.
By the time the buzzer sounded, the team will already have finished the repairs.
items.explanation: The repairs were completed before another past event, the buzzer, so the past perfect had finished is needed. Has finished is present perfect and does not fit a past setting. Finishes is present tense. Will have finished is future perfect and points ahead of the past event.

items.stem:
The Redmond rail museum keeps several restored engines in its main hall. A guidebook describes the oldest one. The first sentence reads: The museum displays a locomotive who was built in 1912.

Which revision uses the correct relative pronoun?
options: The museum displays a locomotive whom was built in 1912.
The museum displays a locomotive what was built in 1912.
The museum displays a locomotive that was built in 1912.
The museum displays a locomotive, that was built in 1912.
items.explanation: A locomotive is a thing, so the relative pronoun should be that or which, not who. Whom is for people and is also an object form. What is not a relative pronoun in standard writing. A comma before that sets off a restrictive clause incorrectly.

items.stem:
A volunteer at the Redmond rail museum wrote the hours for the visitor brochure. The draft is short, and every detail has to be exact. One sentence reads: The museum opens at nine and the first tour leaves at ten.

Where does a comma belong in this sentence?
options: The museum, opens at nine and the first tour leaves at ten.
The museum opens at nine and the first tour, leaves at ten.
The museum opens at, nine and the first tour leaves at ten.
The museum opens at nine, and the first tour leaves at ten.
items.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction need a comma before the conjunction, here after nine and before and. The other choices put a comma between a subject and its verb or inside a prepositional phrase, which splits sentence parts that belong together and misplaces the pause.

items.stem:
The Redmond rail museum offers a guided walk through its historic yard. A visitor wrote in a feedback form about what the tour covered. The sentence reads: The tour includes: the signal tower, the roundhouse, and the dining car.

Which revision corrects the punctuation?
options: The tour includes; the signal tower, the roundhouse, and the dining car.
The tour includes the signal tower, the roundhouse, and the dining car.
The tour includes, the signal tower; the roundhouse; and the dining car.
The tour includes: the signal tower; the roundhouse; and the dining car.
items.explanation: A colon should follow a complete statement, and the words The tour includes cannot stand alone, so no colon belongs there. The list flows straight from the verb. A semicolon in that position is equally wrong. The other choices also use semicolons between simple list items, which need commas.

items.stem:
A retired conductor volunteers at the Redmond rail museum on Saturdays. The museum’s newsletter features him in a profile. One line says: No one knows more about steam engines than him.

Which revision uses the correct pronoun form?
options: No one knows more about steam engines than he does.
No one knows more about steam engines than himself.
No one knows more about steam engines than his.
No one knows more about steam engines then him.
items.explanation: The sentence means than he knows, so the subject form he is needed after than. Himself is a reflexive pronoun with no matching subject. His is a possessive form and does not fit the comparison in this sentence. Then refers to time, while a comparison needs than.

items.stem:
The Redmond rail museum is replacing the roof over the engine hall. The trustees voted at their last meeting. A line in the minutes reads: The board of trustees have approved a budget for the new roof.

Which revision corrects the agreement error?
options: The board of trustees have approved budgets for the new roof.
The board of trustees are approved a budget for the new roof.
The board of trustees were approving a budget for the new roof.
The board of trustees has approved a budget for the new roof.
items.explanation: Board is a collective noun acting as a single unit, so it takes the singular verb has. The first choice keeps the plural verb and changes budget to budgets. The second uses are with a past participle, which forms a broken passive. The third uses a plural past progressive form.

items.stem:
The Lakeview library has started a digitization project for its oldest records. A staff member wrote a progress note for the board. It says: The library scanned ten thousand pages in June now the catalog lists every one.

How should the sentence be corrected?
options: The library scanned ten thousand pages in June, now the catalog lists every one.
The library scanned ten thousand pages in June, and now the catalog lists every one.
The library scanned ten thousand pages in June now, the catalog lists every one.
The library scanned ten thousand pages in June; and now the catalog lists every one.
items.explanation: The original is a run-on, since two complete clauses run together with no punctuation. A comma plus and fixes it. A comma alone makes a splice. Moving the comma after now splits an adverb from its clause. A semicolon followed by and is redundant, because a semicolon already joins the clauses.

items.stem:
The digitization project at the Lakeview library uses an expensive scanner. The director wrote about it in the annual report. The draft reads: The scanner, that cost the library twelve thousand dollars, works around the clock.

Which revision corrects the relative pronoun?
options: The scanner, who cost the library twelve thousand dollars, works around the clock.
The scanner that cost the library twelve thousand dollars, works around the clock.
The scanner, which cost the library twelve thousand dollars, works around the clock.
The scanner, what cost the library twelve thousand dollars, works around the clock.
items.explanation: The clause only adds extra information, so it is nonrestrictive and takes which, with commas around it. Who is for people. Removing the opening comma and keeping the closing one leaves the clause half set off. What is not used as a relative pronoun in standard writing.

items.stem:
Staff at the Lakeview library scan fragile newspapers during the digitization project. A technician wrote a short training note. It says: The scanner works good on fragile pages.

Which revision uses the correct modifier?
options: The scanner works well on fragile pages.
The scanner works goodly on fragile pages.
The scanner works more good on fragile pages.
The scanner works best on fragile pages.
items.explanation: Works is a verb, so it needs the adverb well, not the adjective good. Goodly is not a standard adverb. More good is not a standard comparative. Best is a superlative that suggests a comparison with other scanners, which the sentence does not make at all.

items.stem:
The Lakeview library is digitizing picture books as part of its project. A librarian posted an update for parents. It says: The childrens room holds the digitized picture books.

Which revision forms the possessive correctly?
options: The childrens’ room holds the digitized picture books.
The children’s’ room holds the digitized picture books.
The childrens’s room holds the digitized picture books.
The children’s room holds the digitized picture books.
items.explanation: Children is already plural without an s, so the possessive adds apostrophe s, giving children’s. Placing the apostrophe after an added s treats childrens as the base word, which is not a word. The double apostrophe and the s on an s ending are also not standard.

items.stem:
The digitization project at the Lakeview library must protect old pages, which are brittle. The project leader wrote a brief for volunteers. One sentence in it says: Due to the fact that the pages are brittle, each one is scanned in a manner that is gentle.

Which revision is the most concise?
options: Due to the fact that the pages are brittle, each one is scanned gently.
Because the pages are brittle, each one is scanned gently.
Because of the brittle pages, each one is scanned in a gentle manner.
Because the pages are brittle in nature, each one is scanned with gentleness.
items.explanation: Because replaces the long phrase due to the fact that, and gently replaces in a manner that is gentle, so the sentence says the same thing in fewer words. The other choices fix only one wordy phrase, or they add new filler such as in nature or in a gentle manner.

items.stem:
Students at Maple Hill Elementary tend the school garden each spring. A fourth grader wrote a short note for the class journal. One sentence says: The beans sprouted early, therefore the students added a second trellis.

Which revision corrects the sentence?
options: The beans sprouted early, so the students added a second trellis.
The beans sprouted early therefore the students added a second trellis.
The beans sprouted early, therefore, the students added a second trellis.
The beans sprouted early; therefore the students added a second trellis.
items.explanation: Therefore is a conjunctive adverb, so a comma before it creates a comma splice. The coordinating conjunction so can follow a comma and joins the clauses correctly. Dropping the comma makes a run-on. The version with a semicolon is nearly right but omits the comma after therefore.

items.stem:
The school garden at Maple Hill had a big harvest this fall. The principal wrote a thank-you note to the parent helpers. A draft line reads: The principal thanked Ms. Dale and myself for the garden.

Which revision corrects the pronoun?
options: The principal thanked Ms. Dale and I for the garden.
The principal thanked Ms. Dale and her for the garden.
The principal thanked Ms. Dale and me for the garden.
The principal thanked Ms. Dale and mine for the garden.
items.explanation: Both people are objects of thanked, so the object form me is needed, and myself should be used only when it refers back to a subject in the same clause. I is a subject form. Her would change who is being thanked. Mine is a possessive form and does not fit.

items.stem:
The school garden at Maple Hill has carrots ready for picking. A teacher wrote a note for the class newsletter. One sentence says: The students have began to harvest the carrots.

Which revision uses the correct verb form?
options: The students have begun to harvest the carrots.
The students have beginned to harvest the carrots.
The students has begun to harvest the carrots.
The students have began to harvest the carrots now.
items.explanation: The present perfect uses have plus the past participle, and the past participle of begin is begun. Began is the simple past form and cannot follow have. Beginned is not a word. Has does not agree with the plural students, and adding now does not fix the error.

items.stem:
The school garden at Maple Hill is divided into small plots. A volunteer drew up a map for the new students. A sentence in the caption reads: The two plots were divided among the north fence and the shed.

Which revision uses the correct preposition?
options: The two plots were divided amongst the north fence and the shed.
The two plots were divided among the north fence, and the shed.
The two plots were divided between the north fence and the shed.
The two plots were divided inside the north fence and the shed.
items.explanation: Between is used when only two things are involved, and here there are two places, the fence and the shed. Among and amongst are for three or more. Adding a comma does not fix the preposition. Inside changes the meaning of the sentence and the location it describes.

items.stem:
The Maple Hill school garden holds a harvest supper each October. A parent wrote the invitation for the school paper. One sentence says: Everyone in the garden club were invited to the harvest supper.

Which revision corrects the agreement error?
options: Everyone in the garden club were inviting to the harvest supper.
Everyone in the garden club have been invited to the harvest supper.
Everyone in the garden club was inviting to the harvest supper.
Everyone in the garden club was invited to the harvest supper.
items.explanation: Everyone is a singular indefinite pronoun, so the verb must be singular, was invited. Were and have been are plural forms. The inviting versions change the meaning, since the club members receive the invitation rather than give it. The key is the only choice that keeps both the singular verb and the passive meaning.
